title: Energy, Fields and Waves
bigQuestion: If energy can never be created or destroyed, why do we worry about running out of it, and how does it travel from a distant star to your eye?

story.title: A Magnet, a Coil and a Twitching Needle
story.kicker: In a London basement in 1831, a bookbinder's apprentice turned motion into electricity, and the modern world switched on.
paragraphs: Michael Faraday had almost no schooling. As a boy in London he worked for a bookbinder and read the science books that came in for binding. He talked his way into a job washing glassware for a famous chemist and, over twenty years, became one of the finest experimenters alive. By 1831 he was chasing a hunch. Ten years earlier, a Danish scientist had shown that an electric current makes a compass needle swing. If electricity could make magnetism, Faraday reasoned, magnetism should be able to make electricity.

For years it did not work. He set magnets beside wires and coils and watched his meter for a current. Nothing. Then, on August 29, 1831, he wrapped two separate coils of wire around opposite sides of an iron ring. One coil he connected to a battery; the other to a meter with a needle. At the instant he connected the battery, the needle jumped, then settled back to zero. When he disconnected it, the needle jumped the other way. Nothing happened while the current flowed steadily. Something happened only when it changed.

That was the clue. A steady magnet does nothing to a wire beside it. A moving magnet, or a magnetic field that grows or shrinks, pushes electrons along the wire. Within weeks Faraday was pushing a bar magnet in and out of a coil and watching the needle swing with every stroke. By October he had built a copper disk that spun between the poles of a magnet and produced a steady current. It was the first generator. He had turned motion into electricity.

Every power plant on Earth today, whether it burns coal, splits atoms, catches wind or drops water through a dam, ends the same way: something spins a magnet near a coil, or a coil near a magnet. Faraday's twitching needle is the reason your phone charges and the lights on the Chicago skyline come on at dusk. This chapter follows energy from a moving object, through heat and fields, into the waves that carry it, and carry information, across a room or across the universe.
story.think: Faraday's needle moved only when the current was switched on or off, not while it flowed. What does that tell you about what causes a current in the second coil?

lessons.title: Energy of Motion
lessons.mainIdea: Kinetic energy is one half the mass times the speed squared, so doubling speed gives four times the energy.
reading: A car at 30 kilometers per hour dents a bumper. The same car at 60 kilometers per hour can destroy the front end. Speed doubled, but the damage grew far more than double. The reason is *kinetic energy*, the energy an object has because it is moving. Its formula is one half times mass times speed squared. Because speed is squared, doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by four. Tripling it multiplies the energy by nine.

Energy is measured in *joules*, written J. One joule is the energy needed to push with a force of one newton through one meter. It is a small amount, about what it takes to lift an apple one meter. A 1,000 kilogram car at 10 meters per second has one half times 1,000 times 100, or 50,000 joules of kinetic energy. At 20 meters per second it has 200,000 joules. A crumple zone must absorb all of that, which is why crashes at highway speed are so much worse than crashes in a parking lot.

Energy and momentum are different things, though both grow with mass and speed. Momentum is mass times velocity and has a direction. Kinetic energy is a plain number with no direction; a car moving east and a car moving west can have the same kinetic energy. And because energy depends on speed squared, a fast light object can carry more energy than a slow heavy one. A 0.05 kilogram bullet at 400 meters per second has 4,000 joules, more than a 100 kilogram football player at 8 meters per second, who has 3,200 joules.

When work is done on an object, its kinetic energy changes. *Work* is force times the distance moved in the direction of the force, and it is also measured in joules. Push a cart with 20 newtons for 5 meters and you have done 100 joules of work, and the cart's kinetic energy rises by 100 joules if friction is ignored. Brakes work the other way: friction pushes backward over the stopping distance and takes the kinetic energy away, mostly as heat in the brake pads.

words.d: the energy an object has because it is moving; one half mass times speed squared
the unit of energy and work; one newton pushing through one meter
force times the distance moved in the direction of the force

look.title: Kinetic Energy of a 1,000 kg Car
look.cite: calculated from one half mass times speed squared
look.prompt: Each time the speed doubles, what happens to the energy? A crumple zone that can safely absorb 50,000 joules would be enough at which speeds?

check.q: A cyclist doubles her speed. Her kinetic energy becomes
check.why: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so doubling speed multiplies energy by four.

check.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kilogram ball moving at 3 meters per second?
check.why: One half times 2 times 3 squared is one half times 2 times 9, which is 9 joules.

check.q: How is kinetic energy different from momentum?
choices: Kinetic energy has no direction and grows with speed squared
Kinetic energy has a direction and momentum does not
Momentum grows with speed squared and energy does not
They are the same quantity in different units
check.why: Momentum is mass times velocity and points in a direction. Kinetic energy is a plain number that depends on speed squared.

lessons.title: Stored Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Potential energy is energy stored by position or arrangement, such as height in a gravitational field or a stretched spring.
reading: A roller coaster car at the top of the first hill is barely moving, yet it is about to reach its fastest speed of the ride. The energy is there, stored in the car's height. This is *gravitational potential energy*. Near Earth's surface it equals mass times g times height, or mgh. Lift a 2 kilogram book 1.5 meters onto a shelf and you have stored 2 times 9.8 times 1.5, about 29 joules. Let it fall and that stored energy turns into kinetic energy on the way down.

Potential energy is really energy stored in a field. Lift the book and you are pulling it against Earth's gravitational field; the energy lives in the arrangement of book and Earth. The same idea works for electric fields. Pull two opposite charges apart and you store electric potential energy that returns as they snap back. A battery stores energy in the arrangement of its chemicals, which is electric potential energy at the scale of atoms. A stretched spring or a drawn bow stores *elastic potential energy* in the stretched bonds between atoms.

Height is measured from wherever you choose. A book on a shelf has potential energy relative to the floor, more relative to the basement, and none relative to the shelf itself. Only changes in potential energy matter. As the roller coaster drops from a 60 meter hill, it loses about 60 times 9.8, or 588 joules for every kilogram, and if friction is small, gains that much kinetic energy. Setting one half v squared equal to 588 gives a speed of about 34 meters per second at the bottom, regardless of the car's mass.

Hydroelectric dams are potential energy on an industrial scale. Water behind a dam sits high; as it drops through pipes it spins turbines that turn Faraday's generators. Pumped storage plants run this backward, pumping water uphill at night when electricity is cheap and letting it fall during the day when demand is high. A lake behind a dam is a battery, storing energy as height rather than chemistry.

words.d: energy stored by an object's height in a gravitational field; mass times g times height
energy stored in a stretched or squeezed object such as a spring
a set of blades spun by moving water, steam or air
the level you choose to count as zero height

look.title: The First Hill
look.text: A roller coaster is pulled by a chain to the top of a 50 meter hill and released. After that there is no motor. The ride's second hill is 40 meters tall, and its third is 55 meters. A student says the design must be wrong, because the third hill is taller than the first.
look.prompt: Use potential and kinetic energy to explain whether the car can climb the third hill. What would happen if it could not?

check.q: A 3 kilogram rock is lifted 2 meters. About how much gravitational potential energy does it gain?
check.why: Potential energy is mgh: 3 times 9.8 times 2 is about 58.8 joules.

check.q: Where is the energy of a stretched rubber band stored?
choices: In the stretched bonds between its atoms
check.why: Stretching pulls atoms apart against their bonds, storing elastic potential energy that returns when it snaps back.

check.q: Two roller coaster cars, one twice as heavy as the other, drop from the same hill with little friction. Compare their speeds at the bottom.
choices: The heavy car is twice as fast
The light car is twice as fast
The heavy car is four times as fast
check.why: Mass cancels: mgh becomes one half m v squared, so v depends only on height, just as in free fall.

lessons.title: Heat and Temperature
lessons.mainIdea: Thermal energy is the total kinetic energy of an object's moving particles, while temperature measures how fast they move on average.
reading: Where does the kinetic energy go when brakes stop a car? Into the brake pads and discs, which get hot enough to glow on a race track. The energy did not vanish. It became *thermal energy*, the kinetic energy of trillions of atoms jiggling faster. Every object is made of particles in constant motion. In a solid they vibrate in place; in a gas they fly around and collide. Thermal energy is the total of all that microscopic motion.

*Temperature* is different. It measures the average kinetic energy of the particles, not the total. A bathtub of warm water has far more thermal energy than a cup of boiling water, because it has so many more particles, but the cup has the higher temperature. Scientists measure temperature in Celsius or in *kelvin*. The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, the temperature at which particles have the least possible motion. Water freezes at 273 kelvin and boils at 373.

Different materials need different amounts of energy to warm up. The energy needed to raise one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius is its *specific heat*. Water's is high, about 4.18 joules per gram per degree; iron's is about 0.45. That is why a cast-iron pan heats fast on the stove while the water in it takes minutes, and why Lake Michigan stays cool into June and warm into October, softening Chicago's weather near the shore compared with towns farther inland.

Heat, in the strict sense, is thermal energy in transit from a warmer object to a cooler one. It moves three ways. Conduction passes energy through direct contact, as when a spoon in soup warms at the handle. Convection carries energy in a moving fluid, as warm air rises from a radiator. Radiation carries it as electromagnetic waves, which is how the Sun warms your face across empty space. Understanding all three is the difference between a house that is cheap to heat and one that is not.

words.d: the total kinetic energy of all the particles in an object
a measure of the average kinetic energy of an object's particles
a temperature scale that starts at absolute zero; 0 °C is 273 K
the energy needed to raise one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius

look.title: How Much Energy to Warm One Gram by One Degree
look.prompt: Which material warms up fastest for the same energy input? Why might a city on a large lake have milder summers than one surrounded by farmland?

check.q: A swimming pool at 25 °C and a cup of tea at 80 °C. Which has more thermal energy?
choices: The pool, because it has vastly more particles
The tea, because it is hotter
They are equal because thermal energy depends only on temperature
Neither has thermal energy until it is heated
check.why: Thermal energy is the total motion of all particles. The pool's huge mass gives it more, even at a lower temperature.

check.q: What is absolute zero?
choices: The temperature at which particles have the least possible motion
The temperature at which all matter becomes gas
check.why: Absolute zero, 0 kelvin or minus 273.15 °C, is the lowest possible temperature.

check.q: Which is an example of heat moving by conduction?
choices: A metal spoon in hot soup warming at the handle
Warm air rising above a heater
check.why: Conduction is transfer through direct contact between particles, as in the metal of the spoon.

lessons.title: Energy Is Conserved
lessons.mainIdea: Energy changes form and moves between objects, but the total energy of a closed system never changes.
reading: In the 1840s an English brewer's son named James Joule spent years on a stubborn experiment. He let falling weights spin a paddle wheel inside a tub of water and measured the water's temperature with a thermometer he could read to a fraction of a degree. The water warmed. A known amount of mechanical work had become a known amount of heat, every time in the same ratio. Joule had shown that heat is not a mysterious fluid but a form of energy, and that energy can change form without being lost.

This is the law of *conservation of energy*: the total energy of a closed *system* stays the same. Energy can move from one object to another and change from one form to another, but it is never created or destroyed. A system is simply whatever you draw a boundary around: a roller coaster car, a car plus the road, a whole power plant. Choose the boundary and then keep track of every joule that crosses it. If more goes in than out, the energy inside has grown.

The law is a bookkeeping tool. A roller coaster at the top of a 50 meter hill has potential energy. At the bottom, if the track were frictionless, it would all be kinetic. In reality the car reaches the bottom a little slower than that. The missing joules are not gone; they have gone into warming the wheels, the track and the air, and into sound. Add up the kinetic energy, the thermal energy and the sound, and the total matches the starting potential energy.

Conservation is one of the most tested ideas in science. Whenever energy has seemed to vanish, careful measurement has found where it went. In the 1930s, physicists noticed that a certain kind of radioactive decay seemed to lose energy. Rather than give up the law, Wolfgang Pauli proposed an unseen particle carrying it away. The neutrino was detected in 1956. The law held. The mathematician Emmy Noether showed in 1918 that conservation of energy follows from a deep fact: the laws of physics are the same today as they were yesterday.

words.d: the law that the total energy of a closed system stays the same
the set of objects you choose to keep track of, with a boundary around it
a change of energy from one form to another

look.title: Joule's Paddle Wheel
look.text: Joule reported that when falling weights turned a paddle wheel in water, the water grew warmer by an amount that always matched the work done by the weights. He concluded that the mechanical work had been converted into heat, and that a fixed amount of work always produced the same amount of heat.
look.cite: James Prescott Joule, papers of 1845 to 1850, paraphrased
look.prompt: Joule needed a very precise thermometer for this experiment. Why would a small error in temperature have hidden the result?

check.q: A pendulum swings lower and lower and finally stops. Where did its energy go?
choices: Into thermal energy in the air and the pivot, and into sound
It turned back into potential energy
check.why: Energy is conserved. Friction and air resistance transfer the pendulum's energy to heat and sound, not out of existence.

check.q: What did Joule's paddle-wheel experiment show?
choices: Mechanical work can be converted into a fixed amount of heat
Heat is a fluid that flows from hot to cold
Water cannot be warmed by stirring
check.why: The work of the falling weights always warmed the water by the same amount, showing heat is a form of energy.

check.q: Why did Pauli propose the neutrino in the 1930s?
choices: To account for energy that seemed to disappear in radioactive decay
To prove that energy is not always conserved
To measure the speed of electrons
check.why: Rather than abandon conservation of energy, Pauli proposed an unseen particle carrying the missing energy. It was found in 1956.

lessons.title: Why Heat Flows One Way
lessons.mainIdea: Heat flows from hot to cold on its own and never the reverse, and every energy conversion spreads some energy out as waste heat.
reading: Set a hot cup of coffee on a desk and it cools. It never happens the other way: a room-temperature cup never draws heat from the desk and starts steaming. Energy would still be conserved if it did, so the first law does not forbid it. Something else does. The *second law of thermodynamics* says that heat flows on its own only from warmer to cooler, and that in any real process, energy tends to spread out and become less useful.

The reason is probability. Fast-moving particles in the coffee collide with slower ones in the air and share their motion. There are enormously more ways for the energy to be spread evenly than to stay bunched up in the cup, so spreading out is overwhelmingly likely. Physicists measure this spreading with a quantity called *entropy*. Entropy in an isolated system never decreases. You can move heat from cold to hot, as a refrigerator does, but only by spending energy, which spreads out even more heat elsewhere.

This is why no engine can turn heat completely into work. A car engine burns gasoline to make hot gas that pushes pistons, but most of the fuel's energy leaves as hot exhaust and hot metal. Typical gasoline engines turn only about a quarter to a third of the fuel's energy into motion. Power plants that boil water to spin turbines waste heat through their cooling towers. The waste is not carelessness. The second law sets a limit that no design can beat, though better designs get closer.

The second law also explains why energy can be conserved and still run short. When you use a battery, its chemical energy becomes light, sound and heat that spread into the room. Every joule is still there, but scattered among trillions of air molecules and useless for charging your phone. What we actually run out of is not energy but *useful* energy, energy concentrated enough to do work. The Sun, the wind, fuel and a charged battery are useful because they are concentrated. The warm air in a room is not.

words.d: the rule that heat flows from hot to cold on its own and energy tends to spread out
a measure of how spread out energy is; it never decreases in an isolated system
the fraction of energy put in that comes out in the useful form you wanted
energy that leaves a process as heat instead of doing the intended job

look.title: The Refrigerator in a Closed Room
look.text: On a hot day a student props open the refrigerator door to cool the kitchen. The room is closed, with no windows open. The refrigerator's motor hums, pulling heat from inside the fridge and dumping it out of the coils on the back.
look.prompt: Predict what happens to the kitchen's temperature over an hour. Use the second law and conservation of energy to explain your prediction.

check.q: Why does a hot drink cool down but a cool drink never heat up on its own?
choices: Energy spreading out is overwhelmingly more likely than energy gathering together
Cool drinks have no thermal energy to gain
Heat is destroyed as it leaves the cup
Air cannot give energy to liquids
check.why: There are vastly more ways for energy to be spread out than concentrated, so heat flows from hot to cold.

check.q: A car engine takes in 100 joules of chemical energy and delivers 30 joules of motion. What happened to the rest?
choices: It left as waste heat in the exhaust and engine
check.why: Energy is conserved, so the other 70 joules went somewhere: mostly heat, as the second law requires.

check.q: What do we actually run short of when we say we are running out of energy?
choices: Energy concentrated enough to do useful work
check.why: Total energy never changes. What gets used up is useful, concentrated energy, which spreads into low-grade heat.

lessons.title: Where Our Energy Comes From
lessons.mainIdea: Every energy resource is a way of capturing concentrated energy, and each carries its own costs, limits and trade-offs.
reading: Trace the electricity in your outlet backward and you reach Faraday's generator, but what spins it? In the United States, most electricity comes from burning natural gas or coal to boil water into steam. About a fifth comes from nuclear plants, where splitting uranium atoms makes the heat instead. The rest comes from wind turbines, dams, solar panels and a few smaller sources. Illinois is unusual: its nuclear plants produce about half the state's electricity, more nuclear power than any other state.

Each source is a different way of grabbing concentrated energy. Coal, oil and natural gas are *fossil fuels*, stored sunlight captured by plants and sea life hundreds of millions of years ago. They pack a great deal of energy into a small space and can be burned any time. Burning them releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat in the atmosphere, along with soot and other pollution. Their supply, though large, is finite and is not being replaced on any human timescale.

*Renewable* sources are replaced as fast as they are used. Wind and sunlight are free and clean at the point of use, but the wind does not always blow and the Sun sets, so they need storage or backup. Illinois is a major wind state, with turbines across its flat central prairie. Dams provide steady power but change rivers and flood land. Nuclear plants make no carbon dioxide while running and produce large amounts of power from little fuel, but their waste stays radioactive for thousands of years and accidents, though rare, can be severe.

There is no source without a cost, so choosing means weighing trade-offs: price, reliability, land, water, pollution, safety and climate. The mix has shifted quickly. Since the mid-2000s, coal's share of U.S. electricity has fallen by more than half as natural gas, wind and solar have grown. Engineers and voters keep making these choices, and they work best when the numbers on all sides are honest.

words.d: coal, oil and natural gas, formed from ancient living things and burned for energy
an energy source that is replaced as fast as it is used, such as wind or sunlight
electricity made by using the heat from splitting atoms to boil water
a benefit gained only by accepting a cost or drawback

look.title: Sources of U.S. Electricity, 2023
look.prompt: About what share comes from burning fossil fuels? What share makes no carbon dioxide while running? Which of these sources can run at any hour of the day?

check.q: What do coal, natural gas, nuclear and hydroelectric plants all have in common?
choices: Each ends by spinning a generator with magnets and coils
check.why: Whatever the energy source, the last step is Faraday's discovery: motion of a magnet and coil makes current.

check.q: Which is a limit of wind and solar power that fossil fuels do not share?
choices: They only produce power when the wind blows or the Sun shines
They use up a fuel that cannot be replaced
They cannot be connected to the grid
check.why: Wind and sunlight are renewable and clean at the point of use, but they are not available on demand without storage.

check.q: Why is Illinois's electricity unusual among U.S. states?
choices: About half of it comes from nuclear plants
Most of it comes from solar panels
It has no coal or gas plants
check.why: Illinois generates more nuclear electricity than any other state, and it supplies about half the state's power.

lessons.title: What a Wave Is
lessons.mainIdea: A wave carries energy without carrying matter, and its speed equals its frequency times its wavelength.
reading: Drop a pebble in a still pond and rings spread outward. A leaf floating nearby bobs up and down but does not travel with the rings. That is the key fact about a *wave*: it carries energy from place to place while the material it moves through stays put. Sound is a wave in air, ripples are waves on water, and a shake sent down a rope is a wave on the rope. In each case, a disturbance travels; the air, water or rope only moves back and forth.

Three numbers describe any wave. *Wavelength* is the distance from one crest to the next, measured in meters. *Frequency* is how many waves pass a point each second, measured in *hertz*, or cycles per second. *Amplitude* is how far the material moves from its rest position; a louder sound or a brighter light has a larger amplitude and carries more energy. A wave with a large amplitude can do more, which is why a big ocean wave knocks you down and a ripple does not.

Speed, frequency and wavelength are tied together by one equation: speed equals frequency times wavelength. In air, sound travels at about 343 meters per second. A note of 343 hertz has a wavelength of exactly one meter. A note of 686 hertz has a wavelength of half a meter. If the speed is fixed by the material, then raising the frequency must shorten the wavelength. Try it on the site's wave bench and watch the crests crowd together as the frequency rises.

Waves also bend, bounce and combine. Sound reflects off a wall as an echo. Light bends as it enters water, which is why a straw in a glass looks broken. Two waves meeting can add up to a bigger wave or cancel to nothing, a behavior called interference. Noise-cancelling headphones make a sound wave that is the exact opposite of the noise, so the two cancel at your ear. Interference is how scientists know something is a wave at all.

words.d: a traveling disturbance that carries energy without carrying matter along with it
the distance from one crest of a wave to the next
the number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz
how far the wave moves the material from its rest position
the unit of frequency; one cycle per second

look.title: Speed of Sound in Different Materials
look.prompt: A 500 hertz note travels through each material. Find its wavelength in each. Why might you hear an approaching train through the rail before you hear it through the air?

check.q: A cork floats on a pond as waves pass. What does the cork do?
choices: It bobs up and down and stays in about the same place
It travels along with the wave
It sinks as the wave passes
check.why: Waves carry energy, not matter. The water and the cork move up and down while the disturbance passes through.

check.q: A sound wave in air has a frequency of 686 hertz. About what is its wavelength?
check.why: Wavelength equals speed divided by frequency: 343 divided by 686 is 0.5 meters.

check.q: If a wave's frequency is doubled but its speed stays the same, its wavelength
check.why: Speed equals frequency times wavelength. With speed fixed, doubling the frequency halves the wavelength.

lessons.title: Light Across the Spectrum
lessons.mainIdea: Visible light is one small slice of the electromagnetic spectrum, waves of electric and magnetic fields that all travel at the speed of light in space.
reading: Faraday's fields turned out to be able to wave. In the 1860s the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell wrote equations linking electricity and magnetism and found that a changing electric field makes a changing magnetic field, which makes a changing electric field, and so on, rippling outward through empty space. He calculated the ripple's speed and got about 300,000 kilometers per second, the measured speed of light. Light, he concluded, is an *electromagnetic wave*. In 1887 Heinrich Hertz made and detected such waves in his lab, the first radio waves.

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum, about 3 times 10 to the 8 meters per second, so they differ only in frequency and wavelength. Lined up from longest to shortest wavelength they form the *electromagnetic spectrum*: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Visible light runs from about 700 nanometers for red to about 400 nanometers for violet, where a nanometer is a billionth of a meter. Your eye sees only that narrow band; everything else is invisible but just as real.

Each band has its uses. Radio waves carry broadcasts and phone signals because they pass through walls and travel far. Microwaves heat food by shaking water molecules and carry Wi-Fi. Infrared is felt as warmth and used in remote controls and night-vision cameras. Ultraviolet from the Sun tans and burns skin. X-rays pass through flesh but not bone, so a doctor can see a break. Gamma rays, the shortest and most energetic, come from nuclear reactions and are used to kill cancer cells.

Astronomy changed when telescopes learned to see beyond visible light. Radio telescopes map cold gas between stars, infrared telescopes see through dust to newborn stars, and X-ray telescopes find matter falling into black holes. The site's telescope catches visible light, the same band Galileo used, but modern observatories cover the whole spectrum. Each band tells a different part of the story, because different temperatures and processes make different kinds of light.

words.d: a wave of changing electric and magnetic fields that can travel through empty space
the full range of electromagnetic waves, from radio to gamma rays
one billionth of a meter, used to measure the wavelength of light
empty space with no matter in it

look.title: Maxwell Links Light and Electromagnetism
look.text: Maxwell reported that the speed of electromagnetic waves he calculated from electrical measurements agreed so closely with the measured speed of light that he could hardly avoid the conclusion that light itself is an electromagnetic disturbance, traveling through the same field that carries electric and magnetic effects.
look.cite: James Clerk Maxwell, A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field, 1865, paraphrased
look.prompt: Maxwell had never seen a radio wave; Hertz made one 22 years later. What kind of evidence convinced Maxwell before anyone could test it directly?

check.q: What do radio waves, visible light and X-rays have in common?
choices: They are all electromagnetic waves traveling at the same speed in a vacuum
They all have the same wavelength
They all require air to travel
They are all visible to the human eye
check.why: All are ripples in electric and magnetic fields that move at the speed of light. They differ only in wavelength and frequency.

check.q: Which of these has the shortest wavelength?
check.why: The spectrum runs from long radio waves to short gamma rays. Gamma rays are the shortest and most energetic.

check.q: Why can an X-ray image show a broken bone?
choices: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are mostly blocked by bone
X-rays are reflected by soft tissue
Bones give off their own X-rays
X-rays are a kind of visible light
check.why: Bone absorbs X-rays more than flesh does, so bone casts a shadow on the detector.

lessons.title: Light in Packets
lessons.mainIdea: Light also behaves as a stream of particles called photons, each carrying an energy set by its frequency.
reading: Shine light on a clean metal surface and electrons can pop out. That should not have been surprising, since light carries energy. What puzzled physicists around 1900 was the pattern. Dim blue light kicked out electrons instantly, but bright red light, carrying far more total energy, kicked out none at all. If light were only a wave, a bright enough wave of any color should eventually shake electrons loose. It did not. Color, meaning frequency, mattered more than brightness.

In 1905 Albert Einstein proposed the answer. Light arrives in packets, later called *photons*, and each photon's energy depends only on its frequency: energy equals a constant, h, times frequency. The constant is Planck's constant, about 6.63 times 10 to the minus 34 joule-seconds, first introduced by Max Planck in 1900. A red photon has too little energy to free an electron from the metal, no matter how many red photons arrive. A single blue photon has enough. Brightness only changes how many photons arrive, and so how many electrons leave.

This is why the spectrum's order matters for safety. Radio and visible photons carry too little energy to break the chemical bonds in your cells. Ultraviolet photons carry enough to damage DNA, which is why sunburn and skin cancer come from ultraviolet and not from the far brighter visible light. X-rays and gamma rays carry still more, which makes them useful for imaging and cancer treatment and dangerous in large doses. The energy of one photon, not the total brightness, decides what light can do to a molecule.

So is light a wave or a particle? The honest answer is that it is both, in a way nothing in everyday life prepares you for. Interference experiments show waves; the photoelectric effect shows particles. Each photon travels as a wave and arrives as a particle. This puzzle opened the door to quantum physics, and it is the reason a solar panel works: each photon of sunlight that has enough energy frees one electron in the silicon, and the flow of freed electrons is a current.

words.d: a packet of light energy; the particle form of electromagnetic waves
the release of electrons from a metal surface when light shines on it
the number that links a photon's energy to its frequency

look.title: Red Light, Blue Light
look.text: A physics class shines a bright red lamp at a metal plate for a full minute. A meter shows no electrons leaving. Then they shine a dim violet lamp on the same plate, and electrons start leaving at once. Turning up the violet lamp makes more electrons leave, but each one has the same energy as before.
look.prompt: Explain every part of this result using photons. What would you predict for a very bright ultraviolet lamp?

check.q: What determines the energy of a single photon?
check.why: Photon energy equals Planck's constant times frequency. Brightness changes only how many photons arrive.

check.q: Why does ultraviolet light cause sunburn while brighter visible light does not?
choices: Each ultraviolet photon has enough energy to damage molecules in skin
Visible light is reflected by skin
check.why: Damage depends on the energy per photon. Ultraviolet photons carry enough to break bonds in DNA; visible photons do not.

check.q: Which observation showed that light behaves as particles?
choices: Dim blue light freed electrons from metal while bright red light freed none
Light bends when it enters water
Two beams of light can cancel each other
Light travels at 300,000 kilometers per second
check.why: Only the photon picture explains why frequency, not brightness, decides whether electrons are released.

lessons.title: Electricity from Motion
lessons.mainIdea: A changing magnetic field pushes current through a wire, which is how every generator turns motion into electricity.
reading: Faraday's twitching needle became the law of *electromagnetic induction*: a changing magnetic field through a loop of wire creates a voltage that drives a current. Move a magnet into a coil and current flows one way; pull it out and current flows the other way; hold it still and nothing happens. Faster motion, a stronger magnet or more turns of wire all give a bigger push. The reverse works too. Current in a coil makes a magnetic field, which is how an electromagnet, a doorbell and an electric motor work.

A *generator* is a coil spun inside a magnetic field, or a magnet spun inside a coil. As it turns, the field through the coil grows, shrinks and reverses, so the current flows back and forth. This is alternating current, the kind in wall outlets, which in the United States reverses 60 times per second. A bicycle dynamo, a wind turbine and the generators at a nuclear plant are the same machine at different sizes. What differs is only what does the spinning.

Induction also makes the grid possible. A *transformer* is two coils on an iron ring, Faraday's original 1831 setup. Alternating current in one coil makes a changing field that induces current in the other. With more turns on the second coil, the voltage rises; with fewer, it drops. Power lines carry electricity at hundreds of thousands of volts, because high voltage means low current and less energy lost as heat in the wires. Transformers step it down to 120 volts before it reaches your outlet.

Induction is everywhere once you know to look. An induction cooktop uses a changing field to induce currents directly in the steel of a pan, heating it while the glass surface stays cool. A wireless phone charger is a small transformer with an air gap. The card reader at a store's checkout and the magnetic strip on a transit card both rely on it. Faraday was once asked what use his discovery was. The answer turned out to be almost everything.

words.d: the creation of a current in a wire by a changing magnetic field
a machine that spins a coil and magnet past each other to make electricity
two coils on an iron core that raise or lower an alternating voltage
current that reverses direction many times each second

look.title: Faraday's Goal in His Notebook
look.text: In his laboratory notebook, years before he succeeded, Faraday wrote himself a short reminder of what he was after: to convert magnetism into electricity. When he finally did it in 1831, he recorded that the meter's needle moved only at the moments the current in the first coil was switched on or off.
look.cite: Michael Faraday, laboratory notebooks, 1822 and 1831, paraphrased
look.prompt: Faraday failed for about ten years before the ring experiment worked. What was different about the ring experiment that finally let him see the effect?

check.q: A magnet sits motionless inside a coil connected to a meter. What does the meter show?
choices: A current that grows over time
check.why: Induction needs a changing magnetic field. A still magnet makes a constant field and no current.

check.q: What do a wind turbine and a nuclear power plant have in common?
choices: Both spin a generator to make electricity by induction
check.why: Different energy sources do the spinning, but the last step, a coil and magnet turning past each other, is the same.

check.q: Why do power lines carry electricity at very high voltage?
choices: High voltage means low current, so less energy is lost as heat in the wires
It keeps birds off the lines
check.why: Heat loss in a wire grows with current. Raising the voltage lowers the current for the same power.

lessons.title: Waves That Carry Information
lessons.mainIdea: Any wave can carry a message if you vary it in a pattern, and digital signals of ones and zeros travel farther and cleaner than analog ones.
reading: On May 24, 1844, Samuel Morse sat in the United States Capitol and tapped a key. Forty miles away in Baltimore, an electromagnet clicked in the same pattern, spelling out the first official telegraph message in dots and dashes. It was the first time information had traveled faster than a person could carry it. The idea was simple: switch a current on and off in a code. Every message since, whether a phone call, a photo or a video stream, is the same idea with a faster switch.

Any wave can carry information if you change it in a pattern the receiver can read. An AM radio station varies the *amplitude* of its wave; FM varies the frequency. Your voice on a phone is turned into a pattern of electrical signals and back. A signal that copies the shape of the original sound, rising and falling smoothly, is called *analog*. Analog signals are easy to make, but every bit of static or fading along the way gets added to the message, and each copy is a little worse than the last.

Modern signals are *digital*. The sound or image is measured thousands of times per second and each measurement is written as a number in ones and zeros, the *bits*. A compact disc, for example, samples sound 44,100 times per second. The receiver only has to tell a one from a zero, so small static does not change the message, and a copy is perfect. Errors can be found and fixed with extra check bits. That is why a photo can cross the world through dozens of machines and arrive unchanged.

The bits ride on whatever wave is handy. Cell phones use microwaves. Wi-Fi uses microwaves at about 2.4 and 5 gigahertz. Most long-distance internet traffic travels as pulses of infrared light inside glass fibers thinner than a hair, bouncing along the inside of the glass for many kilometers before it needs a boost. Spacecraft send digital pictures home by radio from billions of kilometers away, so faint that the signal is weaker than a watch battery by the time it reaches Earth, and the bits still come through.

words.d: a signal that copies the smooth shape of the original sound or image
a signal made of numbers written as ones and zeros
one binary digit, a one or a zero; the smallest unit of digital information
a thin strand of glass that carries light pulses over long distances

look.title: The First Telegraph Message
look.cite: Samuel F. B. Morse, telegraph message from Washington to Baltimore, May 24, 1844
look.prompt: Morse sent this as a pattern of dots and dashes over a wire. In what sense was this the first digital signal? What did it have in common with a text message today?

check.q: What is the main advantage of a digital signal over an analog one?
choices: Small amounts of static do not change the message, so copies are exact
It does not need a wave to carry it
check.why: The receiver only needs to tell ones from zeros, so noise below that level is ignored and errors can be corrected.

check.q: How does an AM radio station put a voice onto its wave?
choices: It varies the amplitude of the wave in the pattern of the sound
It changes the speed of the wave
It switches the wave on and off in Morse code
It changes the color of the wave
check.why: AM stands for amplitude modulation: the strength of the carrier wave rises and falls with the sound.

check.q: Most long-distance internet traffic travels as
choices: pulses of light inside glass fibers
check.why: Optical fibers carry digital light pulses for many kilometers with very little loss.

review.q: A car's speed triples. Its kinetic energy becomes
review.why: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so tripling speed multiplies energy by nine.

review.q: A 2 kilogram ball is dropped from 5 meters. About how much kinetic energy does it have just before it lands, ignoring air?
review.why: Potential energy mgh is 2 times 9.8 times 5, about 98 joules, and it all becomes kinetic energy.

review.q: Which statement about temperature and thermal energy is correct?
choices: Temperature measures average particle energy; thermal energy measures the total
They are two names for the same thing
Thermal energy measures average particle energy; temperature measures the total
review.why: A large cool object can hold more thermal energy than a small hot one because it has more particles.

review.q: Why can no engine turn all of its fuel's energy into motion?
choices: The second law requires some energy to spread out as waste heat
Fuel contains less energy than it seems
Motion is not a form of energy
review.why: Energy is conserved, but the second law says every real process spreads some energy into less useful heat.

review.q: A wave on a rope has a speed of 12 meters per second and a wavelength of 3 meters. What is its frequency?
review.why: Frequency equals speed divided by wavelength: 12 divided by 3 is 4 hertz.

review.q: Which lists electromagnetic waves from longest to shortest wavelength?
review.why: Radio waves are the longest, and wavelength shrinks through infrared, visible and ultraviolet to X-rays and gamma rays.

review.q: What did Faraday find was needed to make a current in a coil of wire?
choices: A magnetic field that changes over time
A strong magnet held very still
A steady current in a nearby coil
review.why: Induction happens only while the magnetic field through the coil is changing, which is why his needle jumped only at switch-on and switch-off.

review.q: A photo sent across the internet arrives identical to the original. Which feature of digital signals explains this?
choices: The receiver only needs to tell ones from zeros, and errors can be corrected
Digital signals do not use waves
Digital signals are louder than analog ones
review.why: Noise smaller than the gap between a one and a zero is ignored, and check bits catch the rest.
